source_text: Etsi apud plurimos vestrum, fratres dilectissimi, mens solida est et fides firma et anima devota, quae ad praesentis mortalitatis copiam non movetur, sed tamquam petra fortis et stabilis turbidos impetus mundi et violentos saeculi fluctus frangit potius ipsa nec frangitur, et tentationibus non vincitur, sed probatur, tamen quia animadverto in plebe quosdam vel imbecillitate animi, vel fidei parvitate, vel dulcedine saecularis vitae, vel sexus mollitie, vel, quod majus est, veritatis errore minus stare fortiter nec pectoris sui divinum atque invictum robur exercere, dissimulanda res non fuit nec tacenda quo minus quantum nostra mediocritas sufficit, vigore pleno et sermone de dominica lectione concepto delicatae mentis ignavia comprimatur, et qui homo Dei et Christi esse jam coepit, Deo et Christo dignus habeatur. Agnoscere enim se debet, fratres dilectissimi, qui Deo militat, qui positus in coelestibus castris divinam jam sperat, ut ad procellas et turbines mundi trepidatio nulla sit in nobis, nulla turbatio, quando haec ventura praedixerit Dominus providae vocis hortatu instruens et docens et praeparans atque corroborans Ecclesiae suae populum ad omnem tolerantiam futurorum, bella et fumes et terrae motus et pestilentias per loca singula exsurgere praenuntiavit et cecinit. Et ne inopinatus nos et novus rerum infestantium metus quateret, magis ac magis in novissimis temporibus adversa crebrescere ante praemonuit. Fiunt ecce quae dicta sunt; et quando fiunt quae ante praedicta sunt, sequentur et quaecumque promissa sunt, Domino ipso pollicente et dicente: Cum autem videritis haec omnia fieri, scitote quoniam in proximo est regnum Dei.. Regnum Dei, fratres dilectissimi, esse coepit in proximo. Praemium vitae et gaudium salutis aeternae, et perpetua securitas, et possessio paradisi nuper amissa, mundo transeunte jam veniunt; jam terrenis coelestia et magna parvis et caducis aeterna succedunt. Quis hic anxietatis et sollicitudinis locus est? Quis inter haec trepidus et moestus est, nisi cui spes et fides deest? Ejus est enim mortem timere qui ad Christum nolit ire. Ejus est ad Christum nolle ire qui se non credat cum Christo incipere regnare. Scriptum est enim justum fide vivere. Si justus es, et fide vivis, si vere in Christum credis, cur non cum Christo futurus et de Domini pollicitatione securus quod ad Christum voceris amplecteris, et quod diabolo careas gratularis. Simeon denique ille justus, qui vere justus fuit, qui fide plena Dei praecepta servavit, dum ei divinitus responsum fuisset quod non ante moreretur quam Christum vidisset, et Christus infans in templum cum matre venisset, agnovit in Spiritu natum esse jam Christum, de quo sibi fuerat ante praedictum; quo viso, scivit se cito esse moriturum. Laetus itaque de morte jam proxima, et de vicina accersitione securus, accepit in manus puerum, et benedicens Dominum exclamavit et dixit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secuudum verbum tuum in pace, quoniam viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum; probans scilicet atque contestans tunc esse servis Dei pacem, tunc liberam, tunc tranquillam quietem, quando, de istis mundi turbinibus extracti, sedis et securitatis aeternae portum petimus, quando expuncta hac morte ad immortalitatem venimus. Illa est enim vera pax, illa fida tranquillitas, illa stabilis et firma et perpetua securitas. Caeterum, quid aliud in mundo, quam pugna adversus diabolum, quotidie geritur, quam adversus jacula ejus et tela conflictationibus assiduis dimicatur? Cum avaritia nobis, cum impudicitia, cum ira, cum ambitione congressio est, cum carnalibus vitiis, cum illecebris saecularibus assidua et molesta luctatio est. Obsessa mens hominis et undique diaboli infestatatione vallata vix occurrit singulis, vix resistit. Si avaritia prostrata est, exsurgit libido: si libido compressa est, succedit ambitio: si ambitio contempta est, ira exasperat, inflat superbia, vinolentia invitat, invidia concordiam rumpit, amicitiam zelus abscindit. Cogeris maledicere quod divina lex prohibet, compelleris jurare quod non licet.
pass_a_gloss: Although among very many of you, most beloved brothers, the mind is solid and the faith is firm and the soul is devoted, which is not moved to the abundance of present mortality, but rather, like a strong and stable rock, it breaks the turbulent attacks of the world and the violent waves of the age, and is not broken itself, and it is not conquered by temptations, but is proven, nevertheless, because I notice in the common people some who, either by weakness of mind, or by smallness of faith, or by the sweetness of secular life, or by softness of sex, or, what is greater, by error of truth, stand less strongly and do not exercise the divine and invincible strength of their heart, the thing was not to be hidden nor left unspoken, so that, as much as our mediocrity suffices, with full vigor and with a sermon conceived from the Lord's reading, the laziness of a delicate mind may be suppressed, and he who has already begun to be a man of God and of Christ may be considered worthy of God and of Christ. For he ought to recognize, most beloved brothers, who fights for God, who, placed in the heavenly camp, already hopes for the divine, so that there may be no trepidation in us, no disturbance, when the Lord, with the exhortation of a provident voice, instructing and teaching and preparing and strengthening his Church's people for all endurance of future things, has foretold and sung that wars and fires and earthquakes and pestilences will arise in individual places. And lest the unexpected and new fear of surrounding things disturb us, he has forewarned that adverse things will increase more and more in the last times. Behold, the things that were said are happening; and when the things that were predicted beforehand happen, the things that were promised will also follow, the Lord himself promising and saying: When you see all these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. The kingdom of God, most beloved brothers, has begun to be near. The reward of life and the joy of eternal salvation, and perpetual security, and the possession of paradise, recently lost, are now coming, as the world passes away; now heavenly things and great things are succeeding to earthly and small and transient things. What place is there here for anxiety and solicitude? Who is troubled and sad among these things, except him who lacks hope and faith? For it is his who fears death who does not want to go to Christ. It is his who does not want to go to Christ who does not believe that he will begin to reign with Christ. For it is written that the just man lives by faith. If you are just and live by faith, if you truly believe in Christ, why do you not, going to be with Christ, embrace the promise of the Lord with confidence, and rejoice that you will be free from the devil? Simeon, indeed, that just man, who was truly just, who kept God's commandments with full faith, when he had received a divine response that he would not die before he saw Christ, and Christ, an infant, came to the temple with his mother, recognized in the Spirit that Christ was already born, about whom it had been predicted to him beforehand; and when he saw him, he knew that he would soon die. Therefore, rejoicing about his approaching death, and secure about his near summons, he took the boy in his hands, and blessing the Lord, exclaimed and said: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation; proving, of course, and testifying that there is peace for the servants of God, then free, then tranquil quiet, when, extracted from the world's turmoils, we seek the port of eternal seat and security, when, having completed this death, we come to immortality. For that is the true peace, that faithful tranquility, that stable and firm and perpetual security. Moreover, what else is there in the world, except a battle against the devil, which is waged daily, except a conflict against his darts and arrows, with constant battles? When there is a confrontation with avarice, with impurity, with anger, with ambition, with carnal vices, with secular allurements, there is a constant and troublesome struggle. The human mind, besieged and surrounded on all sides by the devil's infestation, can hardly meet individual attacks, can hardly resist. If avarice is prostrated, lust rises up; if lust is suppressed, ambition succeeds; if ambition is despised, anger exasperates, pride inflates, drunkenness invites, envy breaks concord, and zeal cuts off friendship. You will be forced to curse what the divine law prohibits, you will be compelled to swear what is not allowed.

choices.english: the just man lives by faith

bible_refs.note: Cum autem videritis haec omnia fieri, scitote quoniam in proximo est regnum Dei

pass_b_english: Although among many of you, my dearest brothers, the mind is solid, faith firm, and the soul devoted—unmoved by the present onslaught of death, but like a strong, stable rock breaking the world’s turbulent assaults and the violent waves of the age without being broken itself, unconquered by temptations and instead proven by them—nevertheless, because I see among the common people some who, whether from weakness of mind, smallness of faith, the sweetness of secular life, softness of sex, or, what is worse, error of the truth, stand less firmly and do not exercise the divine, invincible strength of their heart, this matter could not be hidden nor left unspoken. So, as far as my mediocrity suffices, with full vigor and a sermon drawn from the Lord’s reading, the laziness of a delicate mind may be suppressed, and he who has already begun to be a man of God and of Christ may be held worthy of God and of Christ.

For he who fights for God ought to recognize himself, my dearest brothers—he who, placed in the heavenly camp, already hopes for the divine—so that there may be no trepidation in us, no disturbance, when the Lord, with the exhortation of a provident voice, instructing, teaching, preparing, and strengthening his Church’s people for all endurance of future things, foretold and declared that wars, fires, earthquakes, and pestilences would arise in various places (Luke 21:10–11). And lest the unexpected, new fear of surrounding evils disturb us, he forewarned that adversities would increase more and more in the last times (2 Timothy 3:1). Behold, the things that were said are happening; and when the things predicted beforehand come to pass, the things that were promised will also follow, the Lord himself promising and saying: ‘When you see all these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near’ (Luke 21:31). The kingdom of God, my dearest brothers, has begun to draw near. The reward of life and the joy of eternal salvation, perpetual security, and the possession of paradise, recently lost, are now coming as the world passes away; now heavenly things succeed earthly ones, great things small, eternal things transient.

What place is there here for anxiety and worry? Who is troubled and sad among these things, except the one who lacks hope and faith? For it belongs to the one who fears death to be unwilling to go to Christ. It belongs to the one unwilling to go to Christ not to believe that he will begin to reign with Christ. For it is written: ‘The just shall live by faith’ (Habakkuk 2:4). If you are just and live by faith, if you truly believe in Christ, why do you not, as you are about to be with Christ, embrace the Lord’s promise with confidence, and rejoice that you will be free of the devil?

Consider Simeon, that just man who was truly just, who kept God’s commandments with full faith. When he had received a divine response that he would not die before he saw Christ, and Christ came to the temple as an infant with his mother, he recognized in the Spirit that the Christ had been born, the one foretold to him beforehand (Luke 2:25–32); and when he saw him, he knew he would soon die. Therefore, rejoicing at his approaching death and secure in his near summons, he took the child in his hands, blessed the Lord, and exclaimed: ‘Lord, now you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation’ (Luke 2:29–30)—proving and testifying that peace belongs to the servants of God, then freedom, then tranquil rest, when, extracted from the world’s turmoils, we seek the harbor of eternal security, when, having finished this death, we come to immortality. For that is the true peace, that faithful tranquility, that stable, firm, and perpetual security.

Moreover, what else is the world but a daily battle against the devil, a constant conflict against his darts and arrows? We confront avarice, impurity, anger, ambition; we struggle incessantly and painfully with carnal vices and secular allurements. The human mind, besieged and hemmed in on all sides by the devil’s infestation, can hardly meet each attack, hardly resist. If avarice is prostrated, lust rises; if lust is suppressed, ambition succeeds; if ambition is despised, anger inflames, pride swells, drunkenness entices, envy breaks concord, jealousy severs friendship. You will be forced to curse what the divine law prohibits, compelled to swear what is not allowed.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal continuous translation, while Pass B provides a more polished version with necessary scripture citations (Luke 21:10–11, 2 Timothy 3:1, Luke 21:31, Habakkuk 2:4, Luke 2:25–32, Luke 2:29–30) which are required for the allusions/quotes present in the Latin. All clauses, including the complex list of vices at the end, are preserved.
